kzz7yh-a00504-d1e103.summary: Opening of the prologue: because the Sentences pertain to theology, Richard announces that before the proper questions of the book some preliminary questions about theology itself must briefly be treated.
claims: The Sentences belong to theology, so questions about the nature of theology must precede the commentary proper.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e114.summary: First item in the list of nine prologue questions: whether theological teaching is necessary.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e121.summary: Second announced question: whether theology is a science.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e123.summary: Third announced question: whether theology is one science.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e126.summary: Fourth announced question: whether theology is speculative.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e131.summary: Fifth announced question: whether theology is nobler than the other sciences.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e133.summary: Sixth announced question: what the subject of theology is.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e138.summary: Seventh announced question: whether the mode of proceeding in Sacred Scripture is argumentative.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e143.summary: Eighth announced question: how the Sentences stand to theology, whether as a part, as subalternate, or in some other way.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e150.summary: Ninth announced question: whether the mode of proceeding in the Sentences and in Scripture is uniform or different.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e160.summary: First objection against the necessity of theology: teaching about what exceeds natural knowledge is not necessary for us, since Ecclesiasticus forbids seeking higher things ('altiora te ne quaesieris').
claims: What transcends our natural cognition is not necessary for us to seek (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e191.summary: Second objection: philosophy already treats every being sufficiently, including God (metaphysics as 'divine science'), and there is science only of being; so no doctrine beyond philosophy is needed.
claims: Philosophical disciplines sufficiently treat all being, including God (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e207.summary: Third objection: doctrine is needed only to order the soul, and Algazel says philosophy is nothing but the ordering of the soul; therefore only philosophy is needed.
claims: Philosophy suffices to order the soul (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e218.summary: Fourth objection: Augustine roots all sin in disordered love and fear, and Cicero says philosophy heals the soul, frees from desires and expels fears; so philosophy removes the roots of sin and no other doctrine is needed.
claims: Philosophy removes the roots of sin, disordered love and fear (objection).
concepts: philosophy as medicine of the soul

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e237.summary: Argument sed contra from 2 Timothy 3 and 2 Peter 1: scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching, reproving and correcting, and theological scripture is so inspired; hence it is useful.
claims: Inspired scripture is useful for teaching and correction.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e253.summary: Second sed contra: if nature does nothing in vain, much less does God; since theology comes by inspiration of the Holy Spirit, it is not in vain and hence necessary.
claims: God does nothing in vain, so inspired theology is necessary.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e262.summary: Richard's principal reply: theology is necessary chiefly for truths about God knowable only by revelation, and secondarily for naturally knowable truths and for stirring affection. He argues that the end moves as loved and must therefore be known; our end is God as the supremely beatifying good, and knowledge of full beatitude is supernatural (as the failure of philosophers to posit it shows), so a revealed doctrine is needed to know where to direct our life.
claims: Theology is necessary principally for knowing what can only be known by revelation.
The end can only be loved if foreknown.
God as the end of full beatitude cannot be known without revelation.
Philosophers without supernatural illumination never posited full beatitude.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e334.summary: Second part of the reply: theology is also useful for naturally knowable truths about God, since by natural inquiry few reach them, slowly, laboriously and mixed with error, whereas through theology many reach them quickly, easily and without error.
claims: Natural investigation of divine truths is restricted to few, slow, laborious and error-prone.
Theology delivers naturally knowable truths about God more widely and securely.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e352.summary: Third part of the reply: theology is useful for kindling more effective love of God, since philosophy moves the affections only remotely and weakly, while theology presents truths about God that move affection more proximately; and efficacious love in turn aids clearer intellectual knowledge.
claims: Philosophy excites love of God only remotely and weakly.
Theology moves the affections more efficaciously toward love of God.
Love of God helps the intellect to clearer knowledge.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e376.summary: Reply to the first objection: seeking higher things can occur in a diabolical spirit (heretics), a merely human spirit (the presumptuous and curious), or a divine spirit (holy theologians); Ecclesiasticus forbids only the first two, and the same text adds that much above human sense has been shown.
claims: The prohibition on seeking higher things applies only to diabolical or curious inquiry, not to inquiry in a divine spirit.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e397.summary: Reply to the second objection: even if philosophers treated all being, they did not treat it sufficiently, since they could not treat truths about God knowable only by revelation.
claims: Philosophy treats being insufficiently because it lacks revealed truths about God.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e410.summary: Continuation of the reply to the second objection: even regarding naturally attainable truths, the philosophers treated them insufficiently because they mixed in errors.
claims: Philosophers inserted errors even into naturally knowable matters.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e417.summary: Reply to the third objection: philosophy does not adequately order the soul with respect to true, eternal felicity, so theology was necessary; theology even helps toward political felicity more than philosophy, though philosophy, rightly used, does dispose toward future felicity, as Avicenna says.
claims: Philosophy does not order the soul to eternal felicity.
Theology aids political felicity more than philosophy does.
Philosophy rightly used disposes one toward future felicity.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e443.summary: Reply to the fourth objection (Cicero): philosophy frees from desires and fears insofar as they impede political and contemplative felicity, which are felicities only in a qualified sense; Scripture teaches to flee them insofar as they impede true felicity in the vision and enjoyment of God, which cannot be attained by natural powers alone.
claims: Philosophical felicity, political or contemplative, is felicity only secundum quid.
True felicity consists essentially in the clear vision and perfect enjoyment of God and cannot be gained from natural powers.
Theology helps more than philosophy in resisting disordered desires.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e485.summary: First objection against theology's scientific status: a science proceeds from self-evident principles, but theology proceeds from articles of faith that are not self-evident.
claims: Theology's principles, the articles of faith, are not per se nota (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e505.summary: Second objection: there is no science of singulars, yet Scripture narrates deeds of individuals like Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
claims: There is no science of singulars (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e521.summary: Third objection: law commands while science enumerates; Scripture is law (old and new), so it is not science.
claims: Law and science differ, and Scripture is law (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e528.summary: Fourth objection: per Hugh of St Victor faith is above opinion but below science, and conclusions cannot be more certain than their principles; so theology falls below science.
claims: Faith is below science, and conclusions are no more certain than principles (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e542.summary: Sed contra from Augustine (De Trinitate 14): science is attributed to that by which saving faith is begotten, nourished, defended and strengthened, which pertains to theology.
claims: Theology begets and defends faith and so merits the name science.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e556.summary: Second sed contra: that on which all inquiry into truth must be founded is a science; Augustine says the authority of Scripture is the solid foundation from which the mind must not deviate.
claims: Scripture is the foundation of all inquiry into truth.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e574.summary: Richard's solution: theology is a science in the way subalternate sciences are, proceeding not from principles naturally self-evident but from principles known in the light of a higher science, God's and the blessed's knowledge, as optics depends on geometry and music on arithmetic. The articles of faith are those principles. Theology is science simply and, for us, in a qualified way: granting the principles by faith, we know with certainty how the conclusions follow from them. It is less fully a science for us than optics because we cannot acquire the higher science in this life, which reflects the height of its subject matter, not a defect.
claims: Theology is a science subalternated to the knowledge of God and the blessed.
The articles of faith are theology's principles, self-evident in the higher science.
For us, theology yields certain knowledge of the necessary connection of conclusions to believed principles.
Theology's imperfect scientific status for us stems from the transcendence of its object.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e652.summary: Rubric introducing the reply to the first objection, that every science proceeds from self-evident principles (text corrupt).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e659.summary: Reply to the first objection: principles must be self-evident either in natural light or in the light of a higher science; theology's principles, though not naturally self-evident to us, are self-evident in God's and the blessed's science, from which theology receives them.
claims: Theology's principles are self-evident in the light of a higher science.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e675.summary: Reply to the second objection: singular persons in Scripture are not its principal object but are introduced as moral examples, as in moral sciences, and to establish the authority of those through whom revelation came.
claims: Narratives of singulars in Scripture serve as examples and as warrants of authority, not as the principal object of the science.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e692.summary: Reply to the third objection: Scripture is called law because it teaches the observance of law and contains divine law; alternatively it is partly law and partly science, enunciating truths about one subject and precepts ordered to one end, which does not exclude scientific character since law is a practical science.
claims: Scripture's legal character does not exclude its being science, since law is practical science.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e710.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: the objection concerns scientific perfection relative to us, not simply; yet even for us theology participates greatly in scientific character because its principles come with strong testimony, as Richard of St Victor argues in his appeal to the miracles and holy witnesses confirming the faith.
claims: Theology's principles are confirmed by signs, prodigies and holy witnesses, giving it great certitude even for us.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e744.summary: First objection against theology's unity: one science concerns one subject-genus, but theology treats created and uncreated being, which share no univocal genus.
claims: Created and uncreated being share no common genus, so a science of both lacks unity (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e760.summary: Second objection: sciences are divided as their things are; theology treats mutable material things, separated being (God) and human morals, so it seems to be at least three sciences (natural, divine, moral).
claims: Theology seems to contain natural, divine and moral science (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e771.summary: Third objection: theology's unity cannot come from its subject, since it treats all being, nor from its form, since its mode of treatment varies between narrative and demonstrative.
claims: Theology lacks unity of subject and of form (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e782.summary: Fourth objection: the historical narrative parts of theology differ more from the treatment of Trinity and divine essence than natural philosophy differs from moral philosophy, which are distinct sciences.
claims: The narrative and doctrinal parts of theology differ more than natural and moral philosophy (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e801.summary: Sed contra (text partly corrupt): of things ordered directly to one end there is one discipline; everything in theology is ordered to eternal life (John 20), so theology is one science.
claims: Things ordered to one end belong to one discipline.
All of theology is ordered to eternal life.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e823.summary: Second sed contra: metaphysics is one science though it treats all being, so theology's treatment of all being does not prevent unity.
claims: Treating all being is compatible with being one science, as metaphysics shows.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e839.summary: Third sed contra: one science considers the parts and properties of one subject from principles unified in that subject; theology considers God's properties, perfections and effects from articles of faith that have God as subject.
claims: Theology considers God's properties, perfections and effects from principles having God as subject.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e852.summary: Richard's solution: drawing on Aristotle's account of things said in relation to one nature, he holds that a science is one when everything it considers is considered in relation to some one thing. Since a science exists virtually in its principles and conclusions relate to the subject of those principles, a science whose principles share one subject is one; and the articles of faith all have God as subject.
claims: A science is one if everything in it is considered by relation to one thing.
A science is virtually contained in its principles.
God is the single subject of all the articles of faith.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e887.summary: Continuation of the solution: any article of faith cast as a proposition has God as subject (e.g. 'God will raise humans', 'God is the almighty Father, creator of heaven and earth'), so theology is one science.
claims: Every article of faith, put as an enunciation, has God as its subject.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e903.summary: Reply to the first objection: not everything treated in a science is its subject; some things are its parts or properties. In Scripture some are supposita of the subject (the three persons), others properties, operations or effects, all treated in relation to God.
claims: Things treated in a science include the subject's supposita, properties, operations and effects, not only the subject.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e928.summary: Reply to the second objection: diverse things belong to diverse sciences only when they are not considered in relation to one subject of principles; in Scripture everything is related to God.
claims: Diverse things can belong to one science when all are referred to one subject.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e941.summary: Reply to the third objection: theology has unity of subject (God) and also unity of form, since every mode of consideration in it relates to the subject of the articles of faith.
claims: Theology has unity both of subject and of formal mode of consideration.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e954.summary: Reply to the fourth objection, first defect: singular histories are introduced incidentally, as examples and to show the authority of the transmitters of revelation; unity of science is judged by what is principally considered, not what is incidental.
claims: The unity of a science is judged by its principal, not its incidental, contents.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e972.summary: Second defect in the fourth objection: natural and moral philosophy are distinct not merely because their things differ but because they do not consider them in relation to one subject; when things are related to one, numerically (God) or analogically (being), they can belong to one science.
claims: Natural and moral philosophy are distinct because they lack a common subject of reference.
Relation to one, numerically or analogically, unifies a science.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e995.summary: First argument that theology is speculative: Boethius divides speculative science into natural, mathematical and theological.
claims: Boethius lists theology among the speculative sciences (argument).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1013.summary: Second argument: practical science concerns things we can do, but theology concerns God, who does not fall under our operation.
claims: God is not an object of our operation, so theology is not practical (argument).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1020.summary: Third argument: eternal life, the end of theology (John 20), consists in knowing God (John 17), so its end is speculation, and sciences are named from their end.
claims: The end of theology is cognition, so it is speculative (argument).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1033.summary: Fourth argument: the habit of theology's principles is faith, a speculative habit since it dictates what is to be believed rather than done.
claims: Faith is a speculative habit (argument).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1043.summary: Sed contra: the end of speculative science is truth and of practical science action; theology aims at action ('be doers of the word', James 1), so it is practical.
claims: Theology's end is operation.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1054.summary: Second sed contra: theology teaches right living, commands virtues and forbids vices, which belongs to practical science.
claims: Teaching virtue and forbidding vice is practical.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1061.summary: Third sed contra: theology is divided into old and new law, and law is practical science.
claims: Law is practical science.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1066.summary: Fourth sed contra from Gregory's Moralia: Scripture is a mirror for the soul's inner face, showing our progress and moving the weak to imitation, which is a practical function.
claims: Scripture functions as a moral mirror and spur to imitation.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1082.summary: Richard's solution: theology can be called speculative insofar as its subject, God, is not something we make, and practical insofar as it treats our actions; but it is more principally practical, provided praxis is extended to the interior act of the will. Following Avicenna, a science is simply speculative or practical not by its matter alone but by its end; Scripture treats both its non-operable and operable matters chiefly for the sake of operation (love), so all things considered it is more practical than speculative. The essential end of the science, not the incidental intention of the knower, decides the matter.
claims: Theology is more practical than speculative, when praxis includes the will's interior act.
Whether a science is speculative or practical is determined principally by its end, not its matter.
The essential end of a science outweighs the knower's accidental intention.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1150.summary: Continuation of the solution (text somewhat disordered): speculative and practical are distinguished by end rather than matter. That theology is more for operation than cognition appears from what it treats, since its matters about God are maximally lovable and naturally apt to excite affection, and from its mode, which is chiefly hortatory: commanding, forbidding, threatening, promising, giving examples, narrating, and only sometimes arguing.
claims: Theology's subject matter is apt more to excite affection than to illuminate cognition.
Theology's predominant mode is hortatory, suited to moving affection.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1188.summary: Reply to the Boethius argument: by 'theology' Boethius meant metaphysics, the theology of the philosophers, which is indeed speculative.
claims: Boethius's 'theologia' is philosophical theology (metaphysics), not sacred doctrine.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1197.summary: Reply to the second argument: though theology principally treats God, who is not operable by us, it treats him for the sake of love rather than knowledge, since its inspirer prefers to be loved rather than known. Hence speculative matter can be considered in a practical way and vice versa, depending on the ratio, mode and end.
claims: Theology treats God more for the sake of love than of knowledge.
God prefers to be loved more than known.
Speculative matter can be treated practically, and practical matter speculatively.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1226.summary: Reply to the third argument: the knowledge constituting eternal life in John 17 is knowledge that includes love, since perfect knowledge requires perfect love (Augustine, 83 Questions).
claims: The cognition of eternal life is perfect cognition including love.
No good is perfectly known unless perfectly loved.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1237.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: faith is more a practical than speculative habit, extending praxis to love, because we believe in order to love what we believe; and faith is in the intellect insofar as it is moved by the will, which does not fit a speculative habit.
claims: Faith is more practical than speculative.
Faith resides in the intellect as moved by the will.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1258.summary: First objection against theology's superior nobility: certitude belongs to a science's dignity, and other sciences, whose principles cannot be doubted, are more certain.
claims: Other sciences are more certain than theology (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1274.summary: Second objection: first philosophy proves the principles of natural philosophy, but theology does not, so it is not first and hence not noblest.
claims: Theology does not prove the principles of other sciences, so it is not first (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1283.summary: Third objection: the noblest science is wisdom, which is chosen for its own sake, but theology is chosen for the sake of praxis (as established in q.4), so it is not wisdom.
claims: Wisdom is chosen for its own sake, while theology is chosen for practice (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1301.summary: Fourth objection: the noblest science is universal and first, concerning being common analogically to created and uncreated, but theology concerns God; then a sed contra (corrupt text) affirming Scripture's excellence over all human letters.
claims: The most universal science concerns being as common to created and uncreated (objection).
Scripture surpasses all human writings (sed contra).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1320.summary: Sed contra from Augustine's letter to Volusianus: Christian letters are so profound that one could progress in them daily throughout a lifetime of study, implying they are deepest and hence noblest.
claims: Scripture is the most profound of writings.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1333.summary: Richard's solution (opening partly corrupt): theology is nobler than all speculative sciences except God's and the blessed's own, on the two criteria of certitude and excellence of subject. It is more certain because its certitude derives from the unerring light of divine knowledge rather than fallible natural reason. Its subject is better and more wonderful because it treats God as supremely perfect being, chiefly in what exceeds natural reason. Metaphysics treats God only as a being under the analogical notion of being.
claims: Theology is more certain than all sciences, as it rests on the light of divine knowledge.
Theology treats God under the nobler notion of supremely perfect being, whereas metaphysics treats him as falling under being as such.
Revealed truths about God are more wonderful than naturally knowable ones.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1396.summary: Second part of the solution: theology is also nobler than every practical science, since the more dignified practical science is the one to whose end the others are ordered; theology's end is eternal felicity, to which all other ends are ordered, so all sciences are its handmaids (Proverbs 9).
claims: Among practical sciences, the one whose end subordinates the others is noblest.
All sciences are handmaids of theology since their ends are ordered to eternal felicity.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1422.summary: Reply to the first objection: theology is more certain simply, while other sciences are more certain only relative to our weak intellect, which is like the owl's eye before daylight; certitude simpliciter ennobles more than certitude quoad nos.
claims: Theology is more certain simpliciter; other sciences are more certain only quoad nos.
Certitude simpliciter confers greater nobility than relative certitude.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1446.summary: Reply to the second objection: theology judges all other sciences and their principles because it considers the highest cause under the highest aspect; anything in them repugnant to it is to be judged false (2 Cor 10).
claims: Theology judges all other sciences.
Whatever in other sciences contradicts theology is false.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1462.summary: Continuation: theology can also prove the principles of other sciences, and more effectively than metaphysics; e.g. the real distinction of the category of quantity from substance is best proved by the eucharistic article that the accidents of bread remain without its substance.
claims: Theology can prove the principles of other sciences more effectively than metaphysics.
The Eucharist shows that quantity is really distinct from substance.
concepts: real distinction of quantity and substance

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1483.summary: Reply to the third objection: theology is wisdom (Deuteronomy 4), and the conditions of wisdom fit it, the first being that it teaches to know all things as far as possible.
claims: Theology is wisdom.
Theology teaches all things insofar as possible.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1492.summary: Second condition of wisdom applied to theology: it treats matters very difficult for humans to know.
claims: Theology treats things most difficult to know.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1497.summary: Third condition: theology is most certain simply, as shown earlier.
claims: Theology is most certain simpliciter.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1502.summary: Fourth condition: theology considers the absolutely highest cause under the highest aspect.
claims: Theology considers the highest cause under the highest ratio.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1507.summary: Fifth condition: theology is most of all for its own sake, since it is ordered not to temporal things but directly to eternal felicity.
claims: Theology is ordered directly to eternal felicity, not to temporal ends.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1514.summary: Sixth condition: theology is more principal than other sciences, which serve it.
claims: Other sciences are subservient to theology.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1520.summary: Conclusion of the reply to the third objection: these six conditions of the wise come from Aristotle's Metaphysics I. Aristotle's 'for its own sake' does not exclude ordering to felicity, as Avicenna says all sciences are ordered to it; it excludes choosing wisdom chiefly for temporal utility or exterior works. Theology is chosen for the knowledge and love of God, not for temporal things.
claims: Wisdom's being for its own sake excludes temporal utility as principal end, not ordering to felicity.
Theology is chosen for the knowledge and love of God.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1549.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: theology is universal and first because its subject is the absolutely first being, uncreated substance, which is universal in causing and contains the perfections of all beings eminently; hence it considers all being in relation to that substance. Metaphysics is less universal and posterior, treating only what natural light can reach; the priority of being qua being is only a priority in our way of understanding, whereas every other being is really posterior to theology's subject.
claims: Theology is universal and first because its subject is the first substance, universal in causation.
Metaphysics is less universal and posterior to theology.
The priority of being qua being is only conceptual, while God's priority is real.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1587.summary: First objection against God as subject: matter (subject) does not coincide with efficient cause or end, but God is theology's principal efficient cause and end.
claims: Matter does not coincide with efficient or final cause (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1603.summary: Second objection: one must foreknow the quiddity and existence of a science's subject, but per John of Damascus it is impossible to say what God is.
claims: God's quiddity cannot be known, so he cannot be the subject (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1610.summary: Third objection: no science inquires into the existence of its subject, but God's existence must be inquired into somewhere and, per Avicenna, no science is better placed than the highest; so God is not its subject.
claims: A science supposes rather than inquires into its subject's existence (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1623.summary: Fifth objection (numbered fourth): there is no science of the singular, and God is singular.
claims: God is singular and there is no science of singulars (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1631.summary: Objection from authorities: Hugh says the works of restoration are the matter of Scripture, a gloss says the whole Christ, head and members, and Augustine says things and signs; so God is not the subject.
claims: Authorities assign other subjects to theology (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1647.summary: Objection from q.4: theology is more practical than speculative, but if God, who does not depend on our work, were its subject, it would be speculative both by subject and by end.
claims: God as subject would make theology speculative (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1660.summary: Sed contra from Boethius: theology is abstract, without motion and separable, since God's substance lacks matter and motion; thus God appears to be its subject.
claims: Theology concerns immaterial, immobile substance, i.e. God.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1671.summary: Second sed contra: as habit to object, so science to subject; as God is charity's object because all is loved for God, so God is theology's subject because all in Scripture is considered as within divine perfection or as God's effect.
claims: A science's subject is that by whose ratio all its contents are treated.
All in Scripture is treated as part of divine perfection or as God's effect.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1693.summary: Third sed contra from etymology: 'theologia' from theos and logos means speech about God.
claims: Theology by its name is discourse about God.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1700.summary: Richard's solution: God is the subject of theology, though it chiefly considers what cannot be known by natural reason. A science's subject is that whose per se properties it considers, and Scripture considers God's properties and operations: his intrinsic perfection (essential attributes, emanations and properties of the persons) and its shining forth in the works of creation, administration, restoration, sanctification and retribution. The works of creation include the creation, distinction and ordering of creatures.
claims: God is the subject of theology.
Everything in Scripture reduces to God's intrinsic perfection or to its manifestation in five kinds of work.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1743.summary: Elaboration of the works of restoration: prefigured in the Old Law and its sacraments, begun in the Incarnation, advanced in the giving of the New Law, completed in the Passion, made known to a few in the Resurrection, to some angels at the Ascension, and to the whole world through apostolic preaching.
claims: The work of restoration unfolds from Old Law prefiguration to the apostolic preaching.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1759.summary: Works of sanctification are identified as the infusion of virtues and reception of the New Law sacraments.
claims: Sanctification comprises infused virtues and the sacraments of the New Law.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1766.summary: Works of retribution include the last judgment, damnation of the reprobate and chiefly glorification of the elect. By appropriation, power shines in creation, wisdom in administration, mercy in restoration and sanctification, justice in damnation and goodness in glorification. A second argument follows: a science is virtually in its principles, the articles of faith; each article cast as a proposition (e.g. from the Apostles' Creed) has God as subject, so God is theology's subject.
claims: Divine attributes are appropriated to the different works of God.
The subject of the articles of faith is the subject of theology.
Every article of the Creed has God as subject.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1814.summary: Reply to the first objection: the non-coincidence of matter with efficient and final cause holds for the matter that is the subject of change, not for the subject of consideration; it is entirely fitting that God be both subject and end of theology.
claims: The subject of consideration can coincide with efficient and final cause.
concepts: subject of transmutation vs subject of consideration

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1830.summary: Reply to the second objection: the required foreknowledge of 'what it is' is nominal; we know in general what 'God' signifies through his operations, as John of Damascus's etymologies of theos (warming, burning, beholding) show.
claims: Nominal knowledge of quid est suffices for a science's subject.
We know God's quid nominis through his operations.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1854.summary: Reply to the third objection: theology does not inquire whether God exists but supposes it; God's existence under its most general conditions is per se known to us (to be shown later), while special truths about God are revealed and supposed, not inquired into.
claims: God's existence under general conditions is per se notum to us.
Theology supposes rather than inquires whether God exists.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1875.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: there is no science of corruptible singulars, but there can be of incorruptible ones; God is an incorruptible, intellectual singular.
claims: There can be science of incorruptible singulars.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1886.summary: Reply to the authorities: the matter of a science (everything treated in it) differs from its subject (what bears the formal ratio under which all is considered). The works of restoration, Christ and the Church, and things and signs can be called theology's matter while God is its subject, just as Avicenna distinguishes subject from matter in natural things.
claims: The matter of a science differs from its subject.
Restoration, Christ and Church, and res et signa are theology's matter, not its subject.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1927.summary: Reply to the practicality objection: a science need not principally concern something we can make to be practical (in the extended sense); it suffices that its subject is considered under the ratio of motive of the will's ordered love. God as supremely good is supremely lovable, and theology treats God's goodness more principally than his truth, so it remains chiefly practical.
claims: A science is practical if its subject is considered as motive of ordered love.
Theology treats God's goodness more principally than his truth.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1962.summary: First objection against argumentative mode: Gregory says faith has no merit where human reason provides proof, so argumentation would undermine theology's end.
claims: Rational proof destroys the merit of faith (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1980.summary: Second objection: a science had by revelation does not seem to proceed by argument.
claims: Revealed knowledge does not proceed argumentatively (objection).

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1985.summary: Sed contra from Titus 1: the bishop must hold fast the faithful word so as to exhort in sound doctrine and refute opponents.
claims: Sound doctrine includes refuting opponents.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e1994.summary: Second sed contra from 1 Peter 3: be ready to give a reason to anyone who asks for the faith and hope that is in you; so Scripture's mode is ratiocinative.
claims: Christians must be ready to give reasons for their faith.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e2006.summary: Richard's solution: Scripture's mode is manifold: commanding, forbidding, threatening, promising, giving examples, narrating, and sometimes arguing. It does not argue to prove its principles, the articles, but argues from them to other things, except when it proves one article by another, as Paul proves the general resurrection from Christ's (1 Cor 15). This multiplicity does not destroy theology's unity, since all modes chiefly look to divine inspiration.
claims: Scripture's mode of proceeding is manifold, including argumentation.
Scripture does not argue to its principles but from them, except proving one article by another.
The multiplicity of modes does not undermine theology's unity.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e2032.summary: Reply to the first objection: argument proceeding from articles of faith does not lessen faith's merit because it operates in the light of faith; Gregory's dictum concerns reasoning from naturally known principles on which one principally relies.
claims: Argument from articles of faith does not diminish the merit of faith.
Reliance on naturally known reasons can void faith's merit.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e2050.summary: Reply to the second objection: argumentative mode is not repugnant to a revealed science when it argues from believed principles in the strength of supernatural light.
claims: Revealed science can argue from believed principles.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e2064.summary: Opening of q.8, treated without arguments, on how the Sentences stand to theology. Richard distinguishes ways a book relates to a science: first, as an ordered exposition of the letter and sense of the principal book (commentaries on Aristotle, postills on the Bible); second, as an exposition of the sense without following the letter (many writings of the saints, i.e. the Fathers).
claims: A book can relate to a science as literal commentary or as exposition of sense.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e2095.summary: A further mode: a book may contain a science subalternate to another (a music book to arithmetic) or a subalternating science (an arithmetic book to music).
claims: A book can relate to a science through subalternation, as subalternate or subalternating.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e2104.summary: A further mode: a book may contain an ordered extraction of the more useful authorities from the books of a science, as a biblical concordance relates to theology.
claims: Collections of extracts relate to a science as ordered excerpts.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e2115.summary: A further mode: a book may expound the more useful authorities of the books made to explain a science; thus the Sentences relate to the writings of the saints.
claims: The Sentences expound authorities from the writings of the saints.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e2123.summary: Richard's conclusion: the Sentences relate to theology as an ordered collection of useful questions whose solutions are confirmed by reasons and authorities, serving greater understanding of the sense of Scripture. Hence no subject other than theology's should be assigned to the Sentences, just as questions on the Physics share its subject, except perhaps for a difference of reason according to modes of treatment.
claims: The Sentences are an ordered collection of useful questions serving the understanding of theology.
The Sentences have the same subject as theology.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e2148.summary: Opening and answer of q.9: the mode of proceeding in the Sentences and Scripture is neither wholly uniform nor wholly diverse, but more diverse; the Sentences proceed only by argument and inquiry through reasons and authorities, whereas Scripture has many modes.
claims: The Sentences' mode is more diverse from Scripture's than uniform with it.
The Sentences proceed only argumentatively and inquisitively.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e2170.summary: Second difference: when Scripture argues, it does not prove its own principles except one article by another, but the Sentences place articles of faith in question and prove them by authorities, persuasions and valid a posteriori reasons.
claims: The Sentences question and argue for articles of faith, which Scripture does not.

kzz7yh-a00504-d1e2183.summary: Third difference and qualification: Scripture's arguments are subtler and deeper than those of the Sentences, often unrecognized as arguments (Jerome on Job's dialectic). Yet the Sentences' mode is not wholly different, since it imitates Scripture's argumentative mode without reaching it; hence it is more diverse than the same.
claims: Scripture's arguments are more subtle and profound than those of the Sentences.
The Sentences imitate Scripture's argumentative mode imperfectly.

kzz7yh-a00504-Dd1e156.summary: Question 1 holds that theological teaching is necessary. Objections claim that what exceeds natural reason should not be sought and that philosophy suffices to treat all being, order the soul and heal sin. Richard answers that theology is necessary chiefly because our end, God as the source of full beatitude, can be known only by revelation, and the end must be known to be loved. Theology also helps secondarily: it delivers naturally knowable truths to more people, more quickly and without error, and it moves the affections to love God more efficaciously. The replies restrict the ban on 'seeking higher things' to curiosity and heresy. They grant that philosophy has some value but deny that it reaches true felicity, which lies in the vision and enjoyment of God.
claims: Theology is necessary principally for revealed truths concerning the final end.
Theology is useful for naturally knowable truths and for stirring love of God.
Philosophy is insufficient for true felicity.

kzz7yh-a00504-Dd1e481.summary: Question 2 holds that theology is a science. Objections say its principles are not self-evident, that it narrates singulars, that it is law, and that faith falls below science. Richard answers with the subalternation model: theology proceeds from the articles of faith, which are self-evident in the higher science of God and the blessed, as music proceeds from principles of arithmetic. For us it is a science in a qualified sense, giving certain knowledge of how conclusions connect to believed principles; its shortfall from full science comes from the height of its object. The replies explain the narratives of singulars as moral examples and warrants of authority, treat law as a practical science, and ground the certitude of faith in miracles and testimony.
claims: Theology is a science subalternated to divine knowledge.
Its principles are the articles of faith.
Its imperfection as science for us comes from the transcendence of its object.

kzz7yh-a00504-Dd1e740.summary: Question 3 holds that theology is one science. Objections point to its range: created and uncreated being, natural, divine and moral matters, narrative and demonstrative modes, history and doctrine. Richard grounds its unity in reference to one thing. A science lies virtually in its principles; the articles of faith all have God as subject, as appears when each is put as a proposition; so everything in theology is considered by reference to God. The replies distinguish subject from supposita, properties and effects, set incidental narrative content apart from principal content, and explain that natural and moral philosophy are distinct because they lack a common subject of reference.
claims: Theology is one science because everything in it is referred to God, the subject of its principles.
Every article of faith has God as subject.

kzz7yh-a00504-Dd1e991.summary: Question 4 asks whether theology is speculative and answers that it is more practical than speculative, provided praxis is extended to the will's interior act of love. Following Avicenna, Richard takes a science to be speculative or practical by its essential end, not its matter. Theology treats even God, who is not operable, chiefly for love, because its inspirer wants to be loved more than known. Both its matter, which is supremely lovable, and its predominantly hortatory mode show this. The replies take Boethius's 'theology' to mean metaphysics, read eternal life as knowledge that includes love, and classify faith as a practical habit oriented to love.
claims: Theology is principally practical, with praxis including the will's love.
The end, not the matter, determines whether a science is speculative or practical.
Faith is more a practical than a speculative habit.

kzz7yh-a00504-Dd1e1254.summary: Question 5 holds that theology is nobler than all other sciences, divine and beatific knowledge alone excepted. Among speculative sciences it excels in certitude, which rests on the unerring divine light, and in the nobility of its subject, God as supremely perfect being, which metaphysics reaches only as a being. Among practical sciences it excels because its end, eternal felicity, is the end to which all others are ordered, so they are its handmaids. The replies distinguish certitude simpliciter from certitude quoad nos. They claim that theology judges, and can even prove, the principles of other sciences, illustrated by the Eucharist and the real distinction of quantity from substance. Theology meets Aristotle's six conditions of wisdom, and it is more universal and prior than metaphysics because its subject is the first cause.
claims: Theology is the noblest science after the knowledge of God and the blessed.
Theology is more certain simpliciter than other sciences.
All sciences are handmaids of theology.
Theology is wisdom and is more universal and prior than metaphysics.

kzz7yh-a00504-Dd1e1583.summary: Question 6 establishes that God is the subject of theology, though theology chiefly treats what natural reason cannot reach. Two arguments support this. First, Scripture considers God's per se properties: his intrinsic perfection and its shining forth in creation, administration, restoration, sanctification and retribution, to each of which divine attributes are appropriated. Second, a science lies virtually in its principles, and every article of faith has God as subject. The replies hold that subject and end may coincide for a subject of consideration and that nominal knowledge of God suffices. They add that God's existence is per se known in general and supposed by theology, and that science of incorruptible singulars is possible. Restoration, Christ and the Church, and things and signs are reclassified as the matter rather than the subject, and treating God principally as the good keeps theology practical.
claims: God is the subject of theology.
All matters of Scripture reduce to God's perfection or its manifestation in his works.
The matter of a science is distinct from its subject.
Theology remains practical because it treats God principally as good.

kzz7yh-a00504-Dd1e1958.summary: Question 7 holds that Scripture's mode of proceeding is manifold and includes argumentation. It commands, forbids, threatens, promises, exemplifies, narrates and argues. It does not argue to its principles, the articles of faith, but from them, except when it proves one article by another, as with the resurrection in 1 Cor 15. The diversity of modes does not compromise unity, since all rest on divine inspiration. Against Gregory, reasoning from articles of faith in faith's light does not reduce merit; only reliance on naturally known reasons does.
claims: Scripture argues from, not to, its principles.
Argument within faith's light does not diminish merit.
Multiple modes are compatible with theology's unity.

kzz7yh-a00504-Dd1e2060.summary: Question 8 sets out, without arguments, how the Sentences relate to theology. Richard lists the ways a book can relate to a science: literal commentary, exposition of sense (the Fathers), subalternation, ordered excerpts (concordances) and exposition of authorities (the Sentences relative to the Fathers). He concludes that the Sentences are an ordered collection of useful questions resolved by reasons and authorities for the sake of understanding Scripture. So they share theology's subject, God, and differ at most in their mode of treatment.
claims: The Sentences are an ordered compilation of questions in service of theology.
The Sentences share theology's subject.

kzz7yh-a00504-Dd1e2144.summary: Question 9 concludes that the Sentences and Scripture proceed in ways that are partly alike but more diverse than uniform. The Sentences proceed only by argument and inquiry, while Scripture uses many modes. The Sentences put even the articles of faith into question and support them with authorities and a posteriori reasons, whereas Scripture argues only from its principles. Scripture's arguments are also deeper and subtler. The likeness lies in the Sentences imitating Scripture's argumentative mode, though imperfectly.
claims: The Sentences' mode is more diverse than uniform with Scripture's.
The Sentences argue for articles of faith; Scripture argues from them.

kzz7yh-a00504.summary: Article 1 of the Prologue is Richard of Middleton's treatise on the nature of theology, set out in nine questions before the Sentences commentary proper. Theology is necessary chiefly because our end, the full beatitude of the vision and enjoyment of God, is knowable only by revelation (q.1). It is a science subalternated to the knowledge of God and the blessed, with the articles of faith as principles (q.2). It is one science because everything in it is referred to God, the subject of every article (q.3). It is more practical than speculative, with praxis extended to the will's love, since it treats God chiefly as lovable (q.4). It is the noblest science, more certain simpliciter, served by all others as handmaids, true wisdom, and more universal than metaphysics (q.5). Its subject is God, considered in his intrinsic perfection and in his works of creation, administration, restoration, sanctification and retribution (q.6). Scripture argues from its principles among many other modes (q.7). The Sentences are an ordered collection of questions serving theology (q.8), and their mode imitates Scripture's argument while differing from it more than it agrees (q.9).
claims: Theology is necessary because the final end is knowable only by revelation.
Theology is a subalternate science whose principles are the articles of faith.
Theology is one, principally practical, and the noblest science.
God is the subject of theology.
The Sentences are an ordered compilation of questions in service of theology and share its subject.
